title: Putana
hook: a beautiful stranger walks into Nanda's house, smiling, and picks up the baby, and nobody stops her

segments.voice: Yesterday the crossing of the Yamuna came to its end: the girl slipped from Kamsa's hands as a goddess, and Kamsa, after a moment of remorse, chose fear and sent his people after newborns. Your line was stop killing the helpless for nothing. Did you loosen your grip on anything? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

Nanda is away. He has gone to Mathura to pay his dues to the king, and Vasudeva, meeting him there, has warned him: go home quickly, there may be trouble in Gokula. Back in the village, a woman arrives. She is beautiful, the Bhagavata says, with flowers in her hair, a soft smile, a graceful walk. The cowherd women see her and think a goddess has come to visit. She walks straight into Nanda's house, to the bed where the baby is lying. Her name is today's word.
screen: `NANDA IS AWAY.` → `A BEAUTIFUL STRANGER.` → `SHE WALKS TO THE BABY'S BED.`

segments.voice: Putana is one of the killers Kamsa has sent out. The Bhagavata calls her a demoness who goes from town to town killing infants, who can travel through the air and take whatever shape she likes. Today she has taken the shape of a lovely woman. And here is the first unsettling detail. Yashoda and Rohini are right there. They see her lift the child. They are so struck by her beauty and her sweetness that they just stand and watch. The danger doesn't break in. It is welcomed. And the text turns the picture around: Putana takes the child on her lap the way someone picks up a sleeping snake, thinking it is a rope. The danger she doesn't see is the baby. And the child? The Bhagavata says that when she came near, he closed his eyes. The verse doesn't say why. Commentators have offered more than one reason: that he was hiding his power, perhaps, or turning from her cruelty. Putana takes him on her lap and offers him her breast, which she has smeared with poison. And the baby feeds. But he takes more than milk. He draws her very life out with it. She begins to scream: let go, let go. She thrashes, sweating, her eyes rolling. The earth shakes at her cry. And as she dies, her disguise falls away. She collapses in her true form, so enormous that, the text says, trees are crushed beneath her. On top of that terrible body, the cowherd women find the baby, playing, unafraid. Danger came with a smile and was welcomed in. The child knew. And the one who came to feed him poison is undone by the act of feeding.
screen: `A KILLER IN A LOVELY FORM` · `THE MOTHERS JUST WATCH` · `HE CLOSES HIS EYES` · then, large: `"LET GO, LET GO"`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your eyes close if you like, the way the child's did. Breathe in, and bring to mind one thing in your life that arrives looking lovely and leaves you worse: a habit, a feed, a voice, a kind of flattery. You don't need to fight it right now. Breathe out, and simply see it for what it is. Seeing clearly is enough for this sit. If you pray, you can ask in your own way for clear sight. The bell holds the time.
Putana. A killer sent by Kamsa, who comes to the baby as a beautiful woman with poison, and whose life he draws out.
Your line: danger came with a smile. Today, notice one thing that comes to you smiling and leaves you worse, and don't let it walk straight in. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: The killing of Putana is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book and is one of the childhood episodes Hindus retell in songs, dance-dramas and temple art about Krishna.

myth: Putana breaks into the house by force
she walks in smiling, and the women let her pick up the child.
the baby draws out Putana's life as he feeds
she cries "let go, let go" and dies in her true form.
he tells Nanda in Mathura to hurry home, since trouble may come to Gokula.

fork.setup: you're Yashoda. a radiant stranger comes in smiling and reaches for your baby. what happens?
options: you stop her at the door.
you stand and watch, charmed by her.
fork.reveal: the Bhagavata says Yashoda and Rohini were so taken by her beauty that they simply watched her lift the child.

original.note: putana: the name of the demoness sent by Kamsa to kill infants.

trapdoor: what you thought: Putana is a monster story, a demon in plain sight.
what it means: she comes as a lovely woman, and the people guarding the child welcome her in.
what a scholar hears: the text says the child closed his eyes as she came near, and commentators offer more than one reason why.
recall: ate too much and boasted of strength

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.5.20–32: Nanda goes to Mathura, Vasudeva's warning
Bhagavata Purana 10.6.1–18: Putana's arrival, the women's reaction, the poisoned breast, her death in her true form

notes: All paraphrase; 'let go, let go' glosses her cry (10.6.11), not a quotation of a translation.
Confirm: the women take her for a goddess (the text compares her to Shri); the child closes his eyes; the snake-and-rope simile; Yashoda and Rohini watch, overcome by her beauty.
The text gives a size for Putana's fallen body (trees crushed over a distance); the number is left out.
Commentators give reasons why the child closed his eyes; the script names two as possibilities without attributing them. Confirm the verse does not itself give a reason.
Editor pass: corrected the snake-and-rope simile: in the Bhagavata the sleeping snake is the child Putana picks up, not Putana herself.

Audit (2026-10-01): tightened the doubled sentences about why the child closed his eyes. Facts checked against Bhagavata 10.5–10.6; they hold. A Keeper should confirm which commentators give these two reasons.
